newsitem.title: UK: Dlr/mark soft in late Europe, firm mark/yen weighs. [CORRECTED 18:57 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Dlr/mark soft in late Europe, firm mark/yen weighs. [CORRECTED 18:57 GMT]

text.p: The dollar tripped up against the mark in late Europe, upset by gains in mark/yen amid short-covering of yen positions after news of a widening (corrects from 'narrowing') U.S. trade deficit.
Dealers said the trade data pushed dollar/yen higher, lifting mark/yen as trade tension eased ahead of the weekend's G7 summit in Denver.

However, dollar/yen and mark/yen did edge back slightly in late trade following comments by U.S. President Bill Clinton on Japanese television that he was concerned by the rise in the Japan trade surplus.

"The trade figures weren't as bad as expected, so people are not as willing to be short yen into the G7," said a Japanese bank dealer. "Dollar/yen was higher after the data but now it's a mark/yen move, it's purely short-covering at the moment."
Dollar/yen was trading at 114.05/15 after touching a session high of 114.25, well above late Wednesday's level of 113.41/46.
Against the mark, the dollar stood at 1.7254 after touching a high of 1.7365 after the trade numbers, just above late Wednesday's 1.7320/30.
Mark/yen, meantime, pushed to a high of 66.17 before settling back to 66.14/17 and well above 64.45/50 Wednesday.

President Clinton, speaking in a White House interview with Japan's Fuji television network, said he was concerned about Japan's growing trade surplus but understood Japan was taking steps to boost domestic demand.
Clinton also said exchange rates should not be used as a way to correct trade imbalances and the dollar had been strong because of the strength of the U.S. economy.

Earlier today, the U.S. April trade deficit with Japan grew by 5.1 percent to $4.84 billion. The overall U.S. trade deficit grew 7.8 percent to $8.36 billion but this was below an average of forecasts which pointed to a $10.0 billion shortfall.

"The data does suggest the rise in the dollar has not been a problem with competitiveness," said Jeremy Hawkins, chief economist for Europe at Bank of America. "Today's numbers should be view favourably."
Dealers said today's data, even the bilateral deficit with Japan, were not as bad as feared and have taken some of the expected trade friction out of the G7 meeting.
Germany's Bundesbank and the German government announced agreement today on the revaluation of the central bank's currency reserves.
The Bundesbank's dollar reserves are currently valued at 1.3620 marks per dollar giving a total value of 72.3 billion marks.

German government sources said Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer and Finance Minister Theo Waigel agreed a revalue rate of at least 1.50 marks which could lead to a transfer to government finances of over 10 billion marks.
But a Bundesbank spokesman later said no figures on the outcome of a revaluation were decided, nor what level they would be valued.
